clue.text: Initially operate sand to receive invisible creature's head

definitions.text: Initially operate sand to receive invisible creature's head

indicators.note: initially points at the opening letter of each word that follows it in the clue

parts.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Instructions for burying a creature's head in sand so it cannot be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of all seven words spell OSTRICH, and the whole clue pictures the bird famed for hiding its head in the sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular legend says this large flightless bird buries its head in sand to escape danger, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Where the fate of down-and-outs without energy is worked out

indicators.note: worked out suggests something solved or reshaped, so the remaining letters are rearranged
without means the letter for energy is left out of the words that follow

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Where the destiny of the destitute gets decided.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove E from IS WORKED and rearrange. 'Worked out' reads as decided, but 'out' alone is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Skid row is a run-down urban district where vagrants and alcoholics end up, the destination awaiting those who have fallen on hard times.

clue.text: Was 23, having straight lines

definitions.meaning: first meaning: was at the top, i.e. governed
second meaning: marked with lines, like writing paper

explanation.walkthrough: 23 is AT THE TOP, so 'was 23' means held power over others.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule is to govern from the highest position, and ruled paper carries printed parallel guide lines.

clue.text: Arrival includes physical education by an equal

indicators.note: includes means the first word takes the next abbreviation inside itself

parts.note: an arrival is a comer, someone who comes
PE is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A newcomer brings a gym lesson along, courtesy of someone of the same rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A compeer is an archaic or literary word for a peer, companion or person of the same standing.

clue.text: Laughed till bust in 12's 19's situation …

indicators.note: bust means broken apart, so the words before it are smashed and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone laughed until they burst, linked to a bridge's cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is the BRIDGE of 11 12, the Millennium Bridge, and 19 is CATHEDRAL: St Paul's, at the bridge's north end, stands on Ludgate Hill in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: St Paul's Cathedral sits on top of this London hill, so it is the location of the cathedral linked to the Millennium Bridge.

clue.text: Hard as the bed of the one 23?

definitions.text: Hard as the bed of the one 23?

parts.note: surface reading: a mattress that offers no comfort
setter's reading: the one at the top is a monarch, whose head lies troubled

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a bed is as hard as a monarch's.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is AT THE TOP. Shakespeare's Henry IV says 'Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown', so the king's rest is the hard one.
explanation.definitionFit: Uneasy means uncomfortable or troubled, describing both a hard bed and the restless sleep of a ruler.

clue.text: Made like Parmesan, about three points

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the cheese word wraps the compass letters

parts.note: Parmesan cheese is usually served grated
three compass points: east, north, east

explanation.surface: Something was made in the style of grated Italian cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made like Parmesan' runs together, but 'Made' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To generate something is to produce or create it, so generated works as a past-tense synonym for made.

clue.text: Disclose your medieval sports

parts.note: turn up a card to reveal it, plus ye, an old word for you

explanation.surface: A request to reveal your medieval games.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is loose: to turn a card is to show it, and ye is the old form of you, together said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourney is a tournament, the jousting contest knights fought in during the Middle Ages.

clue.text: Hard labour for pirate king having forty winks?

parts.note: Captain Flint is the dead pirate in Stevenson's Treasure Island
K is the abbreviation for king in chess
forty winks is a short sleep, a nap

explanation.surface: A pirate king dozes when he should be doing hard labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard labour' looks like a prison sentence; here it is literally work on a hard stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Flint-knapping is the craft of chipping flint into tools, heavy manual work on a very hard rock.

clue.text: See 5
… whence gnat eats badly worried nine with much umbrage

indicators.note: eats means swallows, so the insect word takes everything after it inside

parts.note: a gnat is a midge, a small biting fly
badly and ill both mean poorly

indicators.note: worried means shaken about, so the number word is jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
most of the word umbrage

explanation.surface: A fly takes offence over the number nine.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on from 5: the Millennium Bridge, a London footbridge, crosses the Thames from below St Paul's on Ludgate Hill. Its 'much umbrage' takes most of a word, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Read after 5, 'whence' means the place from which one crosses: this footbridge starts beside St Paul's and spans the river southward.

clue.text: See 11
Bullish fashion statement?

parts.note: surface reading: a confident, aggressive bit of style
setter's reading: belonging to a bull, whose ring is worn on the face

explanation.walkthrough: Bullish usually means confident; here it means of a bull. Piercings are a fashion statement for people, but bulls are fitted with one for handling.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers put a metal ring through a bull's nostrils to lead it, and people wear the same piercing as adornment.

clue.text: Set to work to make a cheaper engine

indicators.note: make means build or construct, so the given letters are assembled into something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mechanic gets busy building a budget motor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set to work' reads as an instruction to begin; all nine letters are the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-stroke motor has fewer moving parts than a four-stroke one, making it simpler and less costly to build.

clue.text: The poorer nations put their money on the end of the 11 12

parts.note: the global South is the poorer half of the world
to bank money is to deposit it

explanation.surface: Developing countries invest their funds in the far end of a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 12 is MILLENNIUM BRIDGE, which reaches the Thames's South Bank, London's arts district, at its southern end.
explanation.definitionFit: The London footbridge lands on the southern riverside district of the Thames, beside the Tate Modern gallery.

clue.text: Supporters' visits?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stiffening strips in a corset, or ropes holding a mast
second meaning: periods spent as a guest somewhere

explanation.walkthrough: Supporters' looks like fans' visits to an away match; the apostrophe is only surface dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Stays are corset bones and mast ropes that hold things up, and stays are also temporary visits or holidays.

clue.text: Supporters' goose step?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a proud, swaggering walk

explanation.walkthrough: A companion to 16 with the same opening word: 'supporters' again means things that hold up, not fans.
explanation.definitionFit: A strut is a rigid brace in a framework, and to strut is to walk pompously, like a marching parade.

clue.text: Russian girl's farewell embrace of Scottish boy

indicators.note: an embrace hugs someone, so the goodbye word wraps round the name

parts.note: ta-ta is an informal goodbye
Ian is the Scottish form of John

explanation.surface: A Russian girl hugs a Scottish lad goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatiana is a common Russian feminine first name, borne by Pushkin's heroine in Eugene Onegin.

clue.text: Cardinal ends holding a red hat awkwardly in his seat

indicators.note: holding means clasping, so the outside letters go around the rest
ends picks only the outside letters of the churchman word

parts.note: first and last letters

indicators.note: awkwardly means clumsily, so the phrase is put in an untidy new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cardinal sits uncomfortably in his chair with his red hat on.
explanation.walkthrough: A cardinal really does wear a red hat, but here only his outer letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral is the church holding a bishop's throne, the cathedra, so it is literally a prelate's seat.

clue.text: Low sound that's real, not straight from the shoulder

parts.note: a hum is a low droning sound

indicators.note: something not straight is bent or twisted, so the word before is twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A genuine murmur that is not spoken straight from the shoulder, that is, not frankly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight from the shoulder' is an idiom for frankly, but 'not straight' belongs to the wordplay and 'from the shoulder' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Humeral means relating to the humerus, the upper arm bone, or to the shoulder region.

clue.text: Whence helicopters go off to Paris?

indicators.note: go off means explode, so the letters that follow are blown apart and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Where do helicopters depart for a flight to Paris?
explanation.walkthrough: 'go off to Paris' reads as a journey; 'go off' is the explosion and Paris is the material.
explanation.definitionFit: An air-stop is a landing place for helicopters, a stopping point from which such aircraft depart.

clue.text: Letter-writer from twin city whose is opposite the 15

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the apostle who wrote many New Testament epistles

definitions.text: twin city whose is opposite the 15
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Minnesota capital paired with Minneapolis, and the saint whose cathedral faces the South Bank

explanation.walkthrough: 'Whose' means whose cathedral (19): St Paul's stands across the Thames from London's South Bank. Minneapolis and St Paul are the Twin Cities of Minnesota.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle wrote epistles to early churches, lends his name to a Minnesota city, and to London's great cathedral.

clue.text: Matthew's part to play — no amateur in novel room

indicators.note: part says only a stretch from inside the apostle's name is wanted, its outer letters dropped
no says the following word for a non-professional is removed from the word before it

parts.note: the apostle's name
taken as written
taken as written
lay means non-professional, as in a layman

explanation.surface: An actor's role in Matthew's play, with professionals only, in a book-lined room.
explanation.walkthrough: John Braine's 1957 novel is Room at the Top, so 'in novel room' asks for the words that follow 'room' in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title is Room at the Top, so these three words complete the phrase that begins with room.

clue.text: See 27
Put off some French potatoes

indicators.note: some means only part of the phrase is kept, the rest dropped

parts.note: the French for potatoes is pommes de terre

explanation.surface: Someone is discouraged from ordering some French fries.
explanation.walkthrough: Pommes de terre, literally apples of the earth, is French for potatoes; a chunk from its middle is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter someone is to discourage or dissuade them, which is what putting them off means.

clue.text: A vicar forged dead queen's signature — one for the road!

indicators.note: forged means faked or hammered into shape, so the letters are remade

parts.note: taken as written
Queen Anne signed herself Anne R, for Regina

explanation.surface: A clergyman forges a long-dead monarch's signature, then hits the road.
explanation.walkthrough: As shown, A VICAR has a spare I that nothing in the clue removes, so a word was probably lost where the clue has a double space. 'One for the road' usually means a last drink before driving.
explanation.definitionFit: A caravanner travels and holidays in a towed caravan, so is literally someone who belongs on the road.

clue.text: Natter foolishly about feature back on the 15

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the feature word reads right to left
about means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go around the turned word
foolishly means in a silly way, so the chatter word is scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
a dome is an architectural feature

explanation.surface: Silly chatter about some feature at the far end of the bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 is SOUTH BANK, the riverside district opposite St Paul's in London.
explanation.definitionFit: London's modern art gallery, housed in a converted power station, stands beside the Thames on that southern riverside.

clue.text: Victorian writer takes it from Labour politician

indicators.note: takes it from means the two-letter word it is removed from what follows

parts.note: Hugh Gaitskell led the Labour Party from 1955 to 1963

explanation.surface: A Victorian author steals material from a Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests plagiarism; the word 'it' is literally the letters removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote Cranford and North and South during Queen Victoria's reign.

clue.text: Antique pearls provide easy money

definitions.note: money for old rope means easy money, so the answer is what provides it

parts.note: antique things are old
a rope of pearls is a long necklace

explanation.surface: Selling vintage pearls is a nice little earner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Money for old rope' is a British idiom for money earned with no effort.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom money for old rope describes easy profit, so this phrase is what yields effortless earnings.
